description: Structural loads, space frames, Pascal's law, pneumatic vs hydraulic circuits and force calculations.
content_html:
Forces on Structures

Every structure must support and transmit loads — the forces acting on it. Engineers classify loads into two main categories. A dead load is the permanent weight of the structure itself (the steel frame of a bridge, the concrete deck). A live load (also called an imposed load) changes over time — the vehicles crossing a bridge, the people standing on a floor, the goods stacked in a warehouse.

A dynamic load is applied suddenly or changes rapidly — a machine vibrating at high speed, a vehicle braking sharply, an impact during a crash. Dynamic loads are often more damaging than static loads of the same magnitude because the rapid change creates additional stress within the material.

Key Fact

Dead load = permanent weight of the structure (e.g. steel beams, concrete slab). Live load = variable load from use (e.g. vehicles, people, stored goods). Dynamic load = suddenly applied or rapidly changing force (e.g. impact, machine vibration). Cables in a suspension bridge carry tension — NOT compression. This is a common exam error.

Types of Internal Force

When a load is applied to a structural member, it creates internal forces. You need to identify five types:

  • Tension — a pulling force that stretches a member. Cables, suspension bridge hangers and tent guy-ropes are in tension. Cables can only carry tension; they buckle and go slack under compression.
  • Compression — a pushing force that squeezes a member. Stone arch bridges, concrete columns and walls are in compression. Brittle materials (concrete, stone, brick) are strong in compression but weak in tension.
  • Bending — a force that causes a member to curve. A beam supported at both ends and loaded in the middle bends, putting the top surface in compression and the bottom surface in tension.
  • Torsion — a twisting force along a shaft’s axis. A car driveshaft experiences torsion as it transmits engine torque to the wheels.
  • Buckling — sudden sideways collapse of a long, slender compression member (column or strut) under compressive load. A thin aluminium column buckles before the material crushes in compression.

A space frame is a three-dimensional framework of interconnected bars arranged in triangles. The triangle is the only shape that is inherently rigid without requiring rigid joints — any force applied to a triangle is resolved into tension or compression along the members. Electricity pylons, roof trusses and racing car roll cages are all space frames.

A monocoque structure carries loads through its outer skin rather than an internal frame. Monocoque is French for “single shell.” Aircraft fuselages and Formula 1 carbon fibre chassis are monocoque — the shell itself provides rigidity and strength without a separate skeleton inside. This produces very low weight for a given stiffness.

Pascal’s Law and Pressure Systems

Pneumatic and hydraulic systems both use fluid (gas or liquid) under pressure to transmit force. The underlying principle is Pascal’s law: pressure applied at one point in a sealed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions throughout the fluid. This means a force applied at a small piston can produce a much larger force at a larger piston — force amplification.

The pressure equation is: $$P = \frac{F}{A}$$ where \(P\) is pressure in pascals (Pa), \(F\) is force in newtons (N) and \(A\) is area in square metres (m²). Because pressure is equal throughout a sealed fluid, we can write: $$\frac{F_1}{A_1} = \frac{F_2}{A_2}$$ where subscript 1 is the input piston and subscript 2 is the output piston. Rearranging: $$F_2 = F_1 \times \frac{A_2}{A_1}$$

Key Fact

Pascal’s law: pressure in an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions. Force amplification: \(F_2 = F_1 \times \frac{A_2}{A_1}\). A hydraulic system with an output piston ten times larger than the input piston produces ten times the output force. The trade-off: the output piston moves a much shorter distance than the input piston (the fluid volume is conserved).

Pneumatic vs Hydraulic Systems

Both systems use fluids under pressure, but the type of fluid determines the application:

  • Pneumatic systems use compressed air. Air is compressible, so pneumatic systems act quickly but cannot sustain very high forces. They are clean (no fluid spills), cheap to run (air is free) and safe in food and pharmaceutical environments. Typical applications: robot grippers, packaging machines, pneumatic drills, spray painting robots, door openers on trains.
  • Hydraulic systems use hydraulic fluid (oil). Liquids are virtually incompressible, which means the force transmitted is very precise and very high. Hydraulic systems can produce enormous forces in compact cylinders. Applications: JCB excavator arms, car brake systems, aircraft landing gear, forklift truck mast, heavy press machines.

A double-acting cylinder has two air inlets — one on each side of the piston. Compressed air directed to the back drives the piston forward (extend); air directed to the front drives it back (retract). This gives positive force in both directions, unlike a single-acting cylinder that uses a spring to retract.

A 5/2 directional control valve is the standard valve used to control a double-acting cylinder. The “5” means five ports (air inlet, two cylinder ports, two exhaust ports); the “2” means two switching positions (extend or retract). Shifting the valve from one position to the other sends compressed air to one side of the cylinder and vents the other side to exhaust. In an automated system, the 5/2 valve is actuated electrically (a solenoid moves the spool inside the valve) rather than manually.

Worked Calculation: Force Amplification

Daleside Pumps manufactures a hydraulic press for forming sheet steel. The input piston has an area of 0.002 m². The output piston has an area of 0.04 m². The operator applies a force of 150 N to the input piston. Calculate the output force.

$$F_2 = F_1 \times \frac{A_2}{A_1} = 150 \times \frac{0.04}{0.002} = 150 \times 20 = 3000\text{ N}$$ The hydraulic press amplifies the input force by a factor of 20, producing 3000 N at the output piston. Note: the output piston moves 20 times less distance than the input piston (volume is conserved).
exam_tip_html: A very common error: when asked about the force in a suspension-bridge cable or a brake cable, students write “compression.” Cables can only be in tension — they go slack if you try to push them. For hydraulic force calculations, write the formula first (\(F_2 = F_1 \times A_2/A_1\)), then substitute values with units, then give the final answer in newtons. Check you have converted areas to m² before substituting — areas given in cm² or mm² must be converted (1 cm² = 0.0001 m²). Losing a mark here is avoidable with careful unit checking.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Structural loads are classified as dead (permanent weight), live (variable use load) or dynamic (sudden/rapid forces); the five internal force types are tension, compression, bending, torsion and buckling — cables carry tension only, never compression.
  • Pascal’s law: pressure is transmitted equally in all directions in an enclosed fluid. Force amplification: \(F_2 = F_1 \times A_2/A_1\) — a larger output piston produces a proportionally larger force at the cost of a shorter stroke.
  • Pneumatic systems use compressed air (fast, clean, lower force — factory automation); hydraulic systems use incompressible oil (slower, very high force, precise — heavy plant and car brakes). A double-acting cylinder and 5/2 valve are the standard pneumatic control components.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes a dead load on a structure?
A) A load caused by vehicles and people using the structure
B) A suddenly applied impact force such as a collision
C) The permanent weight of the structure itself and fixed components
D) A force that changes direction 50 times per second
practice_questions.marks: C) The permanent weight of the structure itself and fixed components [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
State the type of internal force experienced by each of the following structural members:
(a) A suspension bridge cable supporting the deck
(b) A stone arch in a bridge
(c) A long, thin steel column that collapses sideways under load
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Tension [1 mark — NOT compression; cables only pull]
(b) Compression [1 mark]
(c) Buckling [1 mark]
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A hydraulic car jack has an input piston with an area of 0.005 m² and an output piston with an area of 0.05 m². The mechanic applies a force of 200 N to the input piston.

Calculate the output force produced by the jack.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Calculation: Multi-Step with Unit Conversion
practice_questions.marks:
Formula: F2 = F1 × A2/A1 [1 mark]
Substitution: F2 = 200 × 0.05/0.005 [1 mark]
= 200 × 10 [1 mark for correct ratio]
= 2000 N [1 mark for correct final answer with unit]
[4 marks — method marks awarded even if arithmetic error; penalise if unit missing from final answer]

practice_questions.text: Give two differences between a pneumatic system and a hydraulic system. For each difference, explain how it affects the choice of system for a particular engineering application.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Compare Two Processes or Methods
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Two clear differences, each with an application-linked explanation:
- Pneumatic uses compressible air (fast-acting, lower maximum force); hydraulic uses incompressible oil (precise, very high force). Example: pneumatic for robot grippers and packaging machines where speed matters; hydraulic for excavator arms and car brakes where high force or precision is critical.
- Pneumatic is cleaner (no risk of oil leaks); hydraulic risk of fluid contamination. Example: pneumatic preferred in food/pharma environments; hydraulic acceptable in outdoor heavy plant.
- Pneumatic cylinders extend quickly due to air compression; hydraulic extends more slowly but with greater control.
Both differences must explicitly link to an application.

Secure (3-4): Two differences identified with partial application links. May lack specificity in the application context.

Developing (2): One difference with a brief application link.

Emerging (1): One difference named with no application link.

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the function of a 5/2 directional control valve in a pneumatic circuit that controls a double-acting cylinder.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct point, up to 2 marks:
- A 5/2 valve has five ports (air inlet, two cylinder ports, two exhaust ports) and two switching positions.
- Switching from one position to the other directs compressed air to one side of the cylinder (extending the piston) while venting the other side to exhaust, and vice versa when switched back (retracting the piston).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Marrowbone Engineering manufactures industrial clamping equipment. The design team must choose between a pneumatic clamping system and a hydraulic clamping system for a new metal-forming press that must apply a clamping force of 50,000 N.

Evaluate which system is better suited to this application. In your answer, refer to Pascal's law and the properties of the fluids involved.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Explains Pascal's law (pressure transmitted equally in enclosed fluid, allowing force amplification via F2 = F1 × A2/A1). Shows that both systems can amplify force, but a 50,000 N requirement is very high. Evaluates hydraulic: oil is incompressible — force is transmitted precisely and consistently at very high levels; force amplification is reliable and predictable; used in heavy presses and brakes for these reasons; disadvantage: oil leak risk, higher cost, maintenance of seals. Evaluates pneumatic: air is compressible — force output fluctuates slightly with air consumption; achieving 50,000 N with air pressure alone would require very large cylinder area or very high operating pressure (safety concern); advantage: cleaner, cheaper. Concludes hydraulic is more appropriate for this application with clear reasoning.

Secure (5-6): Correctly identifies hydraulic as better for high-force application. Mentions incompressibility of hydraulic fluid and compressibility of air. Some reference to force amplification principle. Conclusion present with reasoning.

Developing (3-4): States hydraulic is better with a partial explanation of why. May mention force amplification without linking it to fluid compressibility.

Emerging (1-2): Identifies one of the two systems with minimal reasoning.

[8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: A suspension bridge has steel cables holding up the road deck. What type of internal force do the cables carry?
Pascal's law states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted:
options: Equally in all directions throughout the fluid
Only at the point of application

knowledge_checks.q: A load caused by vehicles crossing a bridge is classified as a _____ load.
Hydraulic systems use incompressible oil, which allows them to produce very _____ forces compared to pneumatic systems.
Match each structural term to its correct description:
right: Permanent weight of the structure itself
Sudden sideways collapse of a slender column under compression
Structure in which the outer skin carries the structural loads

flashcard_questions.a: The permanent weight of a structure itself and any fixed components attached to it.
A variable load due to people, vehicles or goods that changes over time.
A suddenly applied or rapidly changing load, such as an impact or machine vibration.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of force does a suspension bridge cable carry?
flashcard_questions.a: Tension only — cables cannot carry compression.
The sudden sideways collapse of a long, slender column or strut under compressive load.
Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions throughout the fluid.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the force amplification formula for a hydraulic system?
flashcard_questions.a: F2 = F1 × A2/A1, where A1 and A2 are the input and output piston areas.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two applications of hydraulic systems.
flashcard_questions.a: JCB excavator arms and car brake systems (accept: aircraft landing gear, forklift mast).

flashcard_questions.q: Name two applications of pneumatic systems.
flashcard_questions.a: Robot grippers and pneumatic drills (accept: packaging machines, train door openers).
A pneumatic actuator where compressed air can act on both sides of the piston, providing powered extension and retraction.
A three-dimensional framework of triangulated members that distributes loads through the whole structure.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are hydraulic systems preferred over pneumatic for very high force applications?
flashcard_questions.a: Hydraulic oil is incompressible, giving precise and consistent force transmission at very high levels.

glossary_terms.definition: A permanent, constant load on a structure due to the weight of the structure itself and any permanently attached components.
A variable load on a structure due to people, vehicles, stored goods or other non-permanent forces that change over time.
A suddenly applied or rapidly changing load, such as the impact of a collision, a hammer blow or machine vibration.
A three-dimensional framework of triangulated members that distributes loads through the whole structure, making it stiff and strong for its weight.
A structure in which the outer skin (shell) carries the structural loads rather than an internal framework; used in aircraft fuselages and Formula 1 chassis.
Pascal's law states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions throughout the fluid.
Compressed air stored in a reservoir and delivered through valves and pipes to actuators; used for lower-force, fast-acting applications in factory automation.
An incompressible oil-based fluid used in hydraulic systems to transmit very large forces with precise control; used in heavy plant, car brakes and aircraft landing gear.
A pneumatic actuator in which compressed air can act on both sides of the piston, allowing the cylinder to extend and retract under power.
